items.stem: Why is respiration considered an exothermic reaction?
items.answer: Respiration is an exothermic process because energy is released during the process.

items.stem: Why do arteries have thick elastic walls?
items.answer: The heart pumps blood at high pressure. If arteries have thin walls they would burst because of high blood pressure. That is why arteries have thick walls.

items.stem: Why are molecular movements needed for life?

items.stem: Explain the significance of peristaltic movement that occurs all along the gut during digestion.
items.answer: It is necessary to move the food in a regulated manner along the digestive tube so that it can be processed properly in each part. The lining of the canal has muscles that contract rhythmically in order to push the food forward.

items.answer: The largest digestive gland in the human body is the liver. It secretes bile juice. Bile juice helps in the emulsification of fats.

items.stem: Name the different types of respiration. Give one example of each.
items.answer:
The different types of respiration are:
(i) Cutaneous respiration: Respiration through skin, e.g., earthworm.
(ii) Tracheal respiration: Respiration through trachea and tracheoles, e.g., insects.
(iii) Branchial respiration: Respiration through gills, e.g., fish.
(iv) Cell surface respiration: Respiration through body surface by diffusion, e.g., Amoeba.
(v) Pulmonary respiration: Respiration through lungs, e.g., human beings.

items.stem: What are the conditions essential for effective respiration?
items.answer:
(i) The respiratory surface should be thin, moist and permeable to oxygen and carbon dioxide.
(ii) The surface should have a large surface area.
(iii) It should be richly supplied with blood vessels for easy transport of gases.

items.stem: What is ATP?
items.answer:
ATP is the source of energy for most of the cellular processes. The energy released during the process of respiration is used to make ATP from ADP and phosphate.
ADP + Ⓟ + Energy → ADP∼Ⓟ = ATP
Here, Ⓟ = phosphate.

items.stem: What is the function of epiglottis in man?
items.answer: The function of epiglottis in man is that, at the time of swallowing food, the epiglottis closes the tracheal opening thereby preventing the food from entering the windpipe.

items.stem: How are the breathing movements controlled?
items.answer: The breathing movements are largely controlled by a respiratory centre located in the medulla oblongata of the brain. This centre is stimulated by the carbon dioxide contents of the blood.

items.stem: Mention the three functions of the nasal cavity of man.
items.answer:
The three functions of the nasal cavity in man are:
(i) It warms the air as it passes over.
(ii) It adds moisture (humidifies) to the air.
(iii) It entraps the harmful particles (filtration) as they pass through.

items.stem: Breathing movements are voluntary or involuntary?
items.answer: Breathing movements are involuntary, but to some extent one can consciously increase or decrease the rate and extent of breathing.

items.stem: Why does the breathing rate increase during vigorous exercise?
items.answer: During vigorous exercise, our body muscles require more energy and as such more oxygen is needed, thus the breathing rate is increased.

items.stem: What is the function of the trachea? Why do its walls not collapse even when there is less air in it?
items.answer: Trachea allows movement of air in and out of the lungs. The walls of the trachea do not collapse even when there is less air in it because these are supported by rings of cartilage.

items.stem: What are the end products formed during fermentation in yeast? Under what condition a similar process takes place in our body that leads to muscle cramps?
items.answer: Ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide are the end products formed during fermentation in yeast. When there is a lack of oxygen in our muscle cells, pyruvate is converted into lactic acid. This build-up of lactic acid in our muscles, during sudden activity, causes cramps.

items.stem:
Lack of oxygen in muscles often leads to cramps among cricketers. Explain why.
Or
When a sportsman runs, he gets muscle cramps. Why?
items.answer: During running, the cricketers (sportsmen) require a large amount of energy instantly. In order to release more energy, pyruvate is converted into lactic acid in the absence of oxygen. Formation of lactic acid in the muscles causes cramps.

items.stem: What product is released after the first step of glucose break-down? Where does it take place?
items.answer: The first step is the breakdown of glucose, a 6-carbon molecule, into pyruvate, a 3-carbon molecule. It takes place in the cytoplasm.

items.stem: During one cycle how many times blood goes to heart of fish and why?
items.answer: One time. A fish has only a two-chambered heart, so blood is pumped to the gills for oxygenation and passed directly to the rest of the body.

items.stem: What is clotting of blood?
items.answer: It is the mechanism that prevents the loss of blood at the site of an injury or wound by forming a mesh into which RBCs get entangled and form a clot.

items.stem:
Briefly describe the shape and function of human white blood corpuscles.
Or
Why are white blood corpuscles called soldiers of the body?
items.answer: Most WBCs or leucocytes are amoeboid, have variously shaped nuclei but lack haemoglobin. WBCs are capable of forming pseudopodia and can squeeze out of blood capillaries to ingest foreign matter. They protect the body from infections. They produce antibodies which are responsible for immunity. That is why WBCs are called soldiers of the body.

items.stem: Briefly describe about the blood platelets.
items.answer: Blood platelets are fragments of cells. They do not possess nuclei. They participate in the coagulation of blood. Blood cells are manufactured in the bone marrow from cells called stem cells.

(ii) RBC contains a respiratory pigment called haemoglobin which carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs.

items.stem: What is blood pressure? How does it vary?

items.stem: Why and how does water enter continuously into the root xylem?
items.answer: Cells of roots are in close contact with the soil and so actively take up ions. The ion concentration increases inside the root and hence osmotic pressure increases the movement of water from the soil into the root, which occurs continuously.

items.stem: Roots of the plant cannot prepare their own food. From where do they get their food?
items.answer: The leaves of the green plant prepare the food by photosynthesis. It is this food which is transported to the roots through the phloem.

items.stem: Why is transportation of materials necessary in plants?
items.answer: The roots of a plant absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil, which are needed by the aerial parts of the plant. As such these substances have to be transported from the roots up to the stem, leaves and flowers. Similarly, leaves of a green plant prepare the food which is needed in all parts of the plant, including roots. This food has to be transported to all parts of the plant.

items.stem: A certain tissue in a green plant somehow got blocked and the leaves wilted. What was the tissue that got blocked?
items.answer: The tissue must be xylem. It is through the xylem that water and minerals absorbed by the roots from the soil are transported to the leaves and other parts of the plant. So, if xylem is blocked, the leaves will not get their nourishment and will wilt.

items.stem: A certain tissue in a green plant somehow got blocked and the roots were deprived of food. What was the tissue that got affected?
items.answer: The tissue must be phloem. It is through the phloem that food prepared by the leaves is transported to the roots. So, if the phloem is blocked, the roots will naturally be deprived of their food.

items.stem: What is phloem? Name its two main components (elements) which help in the conduction of food.
items.answer: Phloem is a conductive tissue which transports the food throughout the parts of a plant. Its two main components are (i) Sieve tube and (ii) Companion cell.

items.stem: What is translocation? Why is it essential for plants?
items.answer: Translocation is the transport of food from leaves to all other parts of the plant, including roots. Translocation is necessary as every part of the plant needs food for harnessing energy and for building and maintaining the organism.

items.stem: What are companion cells?
items.answer: Companion cells are cells which always accompany sieve tube cells and contain a nucleus, cytoplasm and a thin wall.

items.stem: What is the function of the sieve plates in the sieve tube cells of phloem?

items.stem: Name the substances which are transported through phloem to various parts of the plant.

items.answer:

(ii) Water from the kidneys is reabsorbed to maintain the normal concentration of the blood.

items.stem: In winter the frequency of urination is more. Why?
items.answer: In winters the frequency of urination is more because there is hardly any water loss due to sweating, and also because there is no need for the kidneys to reabsorb water. items.answer:

items.stem: What are the final products after digestion of carbohydrates and proteins?
